findings.title: Unbounded work queues provide no backpressure
findings.body: FixedQueuePool builds each work queue as an unbounded `queue.Queue()` and `submit()` never blocks; `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll()` only records a gauge. If a group's single worker falls behind (e.g. one slow subscription), its queue grows without bound while the consumer keeps polling and advancing/committing offsets, consuming memory and risking OOM. The class docstring's claim 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' is therefore false. Use a bounded queue (maxsize) and either block in submit() or stop polling when queues are full.

findings.title: Graceful shutdown abandons queued items instead of draining
findings.body: OrderedQueueWorker.run() tests `while not self.shutdown` *before* calling `queue.get()`. In FixedQueuePool.shutdown() (line 231) every worker's `shutdown` flag is set to True, and only afterwards is `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` called. Because the loop exits as soon as the flag is set, a worker processes at most the one item it had already fetched and then drops everything still queued, so the `immediate=False` drain semantics never take effect. In-flight results are silently discarded on a graceful shutdown. The loop should keep calling `get()` and break only when it raises `queue.ShutDown`.

findings.title: Failed results are still committed and lost (no retry/DLQ)
findings.body: Offset completion happens in a `finally` block, so `complete_offset()` runs even when `result_processor` raises, and `ResultProcessor.__call__` already swallows all exceptions internally. Combined with the offset tracker, a message whose processing permanently fails is still considered done, committed, and never retried or routed to a DLQ — it is silently lost, contradicting the class docstring's 'Only commits offsets after successful processing'. Similarly, submit() (line 317) catches exceptions from decoding/grouping and marks the offset complete, dropping those messages. Errors must leave the offset outstanding (or send to DLQ) rather than be committed.

findings.title: Commit thread stopped before queue drain, leaving work uncommitted
findings.body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread *before* calling queue_pool.shutdown(). Items still drained by the workers after that point complete their offsets but the commit thread is already dead, so those offsets are never committed and the results are reprocessed on restart (duplicates). terminate() also calls the graceful queue_pool.shutdown() rather than abandoning pending work. The queue should be drained/shut down before the commit thread stops, and terminate/close should have distinct semantics (drop vs flush).

findings.title: join() ignores its timeout and can block for ~100s
findings.body: join(timeout) discards the argument and delegates to close(), which calls FixedQueuePool.shutdown(). shutdown() joins each worker sequentially with a hard-coded `timeout=5.0`; with the default 20 queues that is up to ~100 seconds of blocking in the worst case, far beyond arroyo's expected join timeout and potentially past the broker's max.poll.interval.ms during shutdown/rebalance. Respect the passed timeout and join workers against a shared deadline.

findings.title: arroyo Commit invoked from a background thread
findings.body: The commit function passed into create_with_partitions (arroyo's `Commit`) is called every second from a dedicated `commit_thread`, i.e. concurrently with the consumer's poll loop and rebalance handling, whereas every other mode commits from the strategy's processing thread. arroyo's Commit is not designed for cross-thread invocation; if it is not fully thread-safe this can corrupt or lose committed offsets. Either serialize commit calls onto the strategy thread (a lock coordinated with poll/join) or confirm arroyo's Commit is safe to call from another thread.

findings.title: Error-handling test asserts behavior the implementation cannot produce
findings.body: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling patches ResultProcessor.__call__ to raise for the first message and then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that a failed message blocks the commit. But the worker calls complete_offset() in a `finally` even when result_processor raises, so both offsets 100 and 101 are marked complete and are committed; the assertion will fail. Either the exception handling must leave failed offsets outstanding, or the test's expectation is wrong and must be corrected to match the current commit-on-error behavior.

findings.title: test_stats_reporting is racy against active workers
findings.body: test_stats_reporting submits 10 items to a pool with 3 already-running worker threads and immediately asserts `stats['total_items'] > 0`. The workers can consume all items before get_stats() executes, making total_items 0 and flaking the test. Make it deterministic by asserting on a state that cannot race with consumption (e.g. pause/block the workers, or check committed counts rather than instantaneous queue depth).
